summary:
## Getting Started: Installation

This updated RVC process requires no coding (Python, Anaconda) and can run on an external drive. You only need two things:

1.  **The RVC 7z Package**: Download the latest release from the official RVC Project GitHub. There are separate links for NVIDIA vs. AMD/Intel GPUs.
2.  **A File Extractor**: You'll need a tool like **7-Zip** or **WinRAR** to open the `.7z` archive.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> To avoid permission errors, do not extract the archive directly. Instead, create a new, empty folder (e.g., `RVC 2025`), open the `.7z` file, select all its contents, and drag them into your new folder.

To launch the program, simply run the **`go-web.bat`** file. It will open the RVC Web UI in your default browser. If it doesn't, you can manually navigate to `http://localhost:7897`.

## Finding & Using Vocal Models

*   **Source**: You can find thousands of free models on sites like **voicemodels.com**.
*   **Model Files**: A model consists of two files:
    *   **`.pth` file**: The main model weights.
    *   **`.index` file**: Controls the voice's timbre.
*   **File Placement**:
    *   Place the **`.pth`** file in the `assets/weights` folder.
    *   Place the **`.index`** file inside a new, descriptively named sub-folder within the `logs` folder (e.g., `logs/SpongeBob/spongebob.index`).

After placing the files, go to the RVC Web UI and click **Refresh voice list and index path** to load them.

## Key Inferencing Settings

### Vocal Conversion Method
This is the most important setting and depends on your hardware.

> [!TIP]
> *   **Strong/Weak GPU**: Use **`RMVPE`**. It provides the highest quality results.
> *   **No GPU (CPU only)**: Use **`harvest`** or **`PM`**.

### Other Important Settings

*   **Search Feature Ratio**: Controls accent strength. If the AI voice has a strong accent but your source vocal doesn't, you may need to adjust this. Lowering it can reduce artifacts.
*   **Envelope Scaling**: Adjusts how much the AI mimics the dynamics (loudness) of your source vocal. Leave at default unless you have issues with very dynamic recordings.
*   **Voiceless Consonant Protection**: Helps reduce artifacts from breath sounds between words. It's better to manually remove breaths from your source audio before conversion for the cleanest result.

## Tips for High-Quality Results

1.  **Source Vocal Quality**: The cleaner your input recording, the better the output. Export your vocals dry, with no Auto-Tune or heavy effects.
2.  **Model Quality**: A model with a higher **epoch count** (e.g., 1000 vs. 150) is generally trained on more data and will produce a better result. If you're getting poor conversions, try finding a better model for the same character.
3.  **Imitate the Voice**: Attempting to mimic the pitch and accent of the target character in your own performance can significantly improve the final conversion.

## Introduction: The Easiest Way to Use RVC

It's 2025 and converting your own voice into AI vocals has never been easier. You no longer need to learn any Python, Anaconda, or any coding at all, and you don't even need a GPU for the inferencing portion of the vocal.

I'll be trying to make this tutorial as short and simple as possible, and I'll be showing you guys how to install RVC or retrieval based voice conversion, and how to run the web UI locally on your own computer, as well as where to download and how to install the vocal models and the best settings for inferencing or converting your own vocal.

I will not be going over training in this video as that's a little more in-depth, and I'll be making a separate 2025 update for how to train your own vocals within RVC.

## Downloading RVC and Required Tools

First things first, you're only going to need two separate files to install. The first is this 7z file from the RVC project GitHub. If you head to the link linked below and just go down to releases and download the latest release. If you're a Nvidia GPU user, you download this link, and if you're AMD and Intel GPU user, you download this link.

As far as inferencing, you do not even need a GPU, so I believe either link will work for you. And in order to extract a 7z file, you will need to download 7z. A 7z file is basically a formatting version of zip files that's even more heavily compressed. And if you have any worries about 7z, you can also just download WinRAR and it can also open 7z files.

## Installing RVC on Your Computer

So, once you've installed WinRAR or 7z, go ahead and head to your downloads and open up the RVC 7z. One of the benefits of the 2025 version of RVC is you no longer need it on your main hard drive. This means you can run it on external hard drive or any other hard drive that you have attached to your computer.

You don't want to drag this directly into a folder or extract it. When I attempted this before, there was a couple different permission issues when it tried to get the files out of the folder, so I think the easiest way, personally, is to create a brand new folder. We're just going to name it RBC 2025. And opposed to dragging the whole folder here or extracting, we're actually going to open the folder, control A to select all files within, and then click and drag those into the new RBC 2025 folder.

## Launching the RVC Web UI

So, once you have it extracted, this might look a bit overwhelming, but the only file you need to worry about is the go-web.bat. If you click the go-web.bat, it'll open up this command prompt, and just give it a few moments to run and look for your GPU or CPU, and it shall open itself inside of your default web browser.

If it doesn't open up within your default web browser, or if you want to use a different web browser, you can just look at the number here, 7897, and replace the http 0.0.0.0 with localhost. So, I'll show you what that looks like here inside of Google Chrome. localhost:7897. And as you see, it'll open up the web UI within whatever browser you would like.

## Finding and Placing Vocal Model Files

One thing you'll notice is by default, you'll already have some vocal paths here. These are the vocal models that they trained, but we're going to go ahead and download our own. And let me go ahead and show you how to do that. So, there is a website called voicemodels.com, and this website hosts over 118,000 vocal models.

I'm not affiliated in any way with this website, but it is completely free to use, and basically all it's doing is hosting the hugging spaces for other vocal models. So, let's go ahead and download a vocal model. The vocal model I'll be using is a SpongeBob SquarePants vocal model, because I think it is one of the most easy to recognize, and I'm just going to use this 157 epoch version here. It's not going to be the highest quality because of the low epoch count, because basically every single epoch is how many times it ran through the sample set. So, let's say you had 1,000 samples, one epoch mean it means it trained on 1,000 samples. With that downloaded, go ahead and open the zip and you're going to be presented with two files.

You'll have the path file, which is basically the weight that you will get after the data set, and you'll have the index file, which basically controls the the timbre of the voice that you're imitating. And there will be two locations inside of your original RVC 2025 folder that you need to focus on. There is the log section, which is where you will put the index file, and what I like to do is make a brand new folder so that the long string of text isn't difficult to find inside of the actual WebUI. So, we'll just name this SpongeBob, and then we'll drag the index file in. And remember, that is the logs folder within your RVC 2025 folder that we made earlier.

And then next, you just head into assets and then weights, and then click and drag the SpongeBob voice into the folder.

## Loading Your Model into RVC

With that done, you just head back to your RVC WebUI and click refresh voice list and index path. And then you just click into the SpongeBob.path and go down to your auto detect index path and select SpongeBob from the drop-down. If you do not see them, once again, click refresh voice list and index path and double-check that you put them into the correct folders.

## Understanding Key Inference Settings

So, now that we've done that, we can take a look at these five settings here. Resampling should never need to be touched. This is more to adjust the final sample rate. So, say you want it to be 48,000 Hz and it was started at 44,000 Hz, that's what you would adjust there. But, that is not something you're normally going to need to touch at all.

Envelope scaling determines how much it mimics your voice when you're speaking. So, if you're extremely loud person or if there's a lot of peaks within your voice, you might want to lower the sound so it's consistently more loud. For instance, if you're talking up here and then you suddenly get quiet like that, it will have a hard time determining the low points in your voice unless you turn this number down. But, I just leave it at default, personally.

Then this right here protects the voiceless consonants and breath sounds to prevent artifacts. And that basically means it's protecting it from the breathing sounds that will give you distorted vocals between the breaths. Personally, I recommend cutting those breaths out yourself, and I will be making a separate tutorial on how to train properly, and also how to sample your own voice properly, and that should help with any of those issues. I do not recommend messing with this too much because more than likely, if you need to mess with this, you probably have too much breathing in your vocal samples already.

These two are completely fine to ignore. And this is just another breathiness setting, and this has to do with the search feature ratio, which controls the accent strength. Like, for instance, if your initial vocal is an English accent, like, "Hello, mate." And the other person isn't English, then you would want to adjust the search feature ratio. Uh if it's too high, it creates artifacting, so you want to lower that to control the accent strength.

## Choosing the Right Conversion Algorithm

As far as vocal conversion methods, if you have no GPU at all, you want to use harvest or PM. And if you have a weak GPU, you can use RMVPE. And even if you do have a strong GPU, I still recommend RMVPE. It just gives us a much more high-quality sample than if we were to use crepe, which was the previous most powerful algorithm that was available.

## Live Demo: Converting a Vocal Track

So, I'm going to go ahead and record some vocals and show you what they sound like converted. I'm currently working on a AI SpongeBob song, so I'll just give you a quick example of what that is. And if you head to my channel, there'll actually be a full tutorial on how to make AI music, more specific to recording the vocals and matching it to the audio as well.

And when you come here, all you need to do is paste that path right here where it says enter the path of the audio file. And it's okay to leave the quotations here.

Once that is done, all you need to do is make sure you have the correct algorithm selected. And like I said, RMVPE is the easiest and best quality as long as you have some GPU. It does not even need to be a powerful GPU. And if you just have a CPU, you can use harvest or PM. With that selected, let's press convert.

The conversion process takes a little longer the very first time you convert, but it's still very, very quick. But once that's done, you will get the audio here. And all you need to do is click right click and download to download the file. Then you drag this file back into whatever audio program you're working on. And let's go ahead and listen to what that sounds like after it's converted.

And it's literally as simple as that. I hope you guys enjoyed that tutorial.
